fetched_contents.text: CHECKLIST FOR PREVALENCE STUDIES Critical Appraisal tools for use in JBI Systematic Reviews INTRODUCTION JBI is an international research organisation based in the Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences at the University of Adelaide, South Australia. JBI develops and delivers unique evidence-based information, software, education and training designed to improve healthcare practice and health outcomes. With over 70 Collaborating Entities, servicing over 90 countries, JBI is a recognised global leader in evidence-based healthcare. JBI Systematic Reviews The core of evidence synthesis is the systematic review of literature of a particular intervention, condition or issue. The systematic review is essentially an analysis of the available literature (that is, evidence) and a judgment of the effectiveness or otherwise of a practice, involving a series of complex steps. JBI takes a particular view on what counts as evidence and the methods utilised to synthesise those different types of evidence. In line with this broader view of evidence, JBI has developed theories, methodologies and rigorous processes for the critical appraisal and synthesis of these diverse forms of evidence in order to aid in clinical decision-making in healthcare. There now exists JBI guidance for conducting reviews of effectiveness research, qualitative research, prevalence/incidence, etiology/risk, economic evaluations, text/opinion, diagnostic test accuracy, mixed-methods, umbrella reviews and scoping reviews. Further information regarding JBI systematic reviews can be found in the JBI Evidence Synthesis Manual. JBI Critical Appraisal Tools All systematic reviews incorporate a process of critique or appraisal of the research evidence. The purpose of this appraisal is to assess the methodological quality of a study and to determine the extent to which a study has addressed the possibility of bias in its design, conduct and analysis. All papers selected for inclusion in the systematic review (that is - those that meet the inclusion criteria described in the protocol) need to be subjected to rigorous appraisal by two critical appraisers. The results of this appraisal can then be used to inform synthesis and interpretation of the results of the study. JBI Critical appraisal tools have been developed by the JBI and collaborators and approved by the JBI Scientific Committee following extensive peer review. Although designed for use in systematic reviews, JBI critical appraisal tools can also be used when creating Critically Appraised Topics (CAT), in journal clubs and as an educational tool. Practical steps for incorporating JBI appraisal into prevalence study evaluation

The JBI approach to appraisal is structured around a checklist that asks reviewers to judge each item as “Yes,” “No,” “Unclear,” or “Not applicable,” with the goal of assessing methodological quality and bias risk [N1-F1][N1-F2]. For prevalence studies, the checklist is explicit about design and reporting quality, but it also relies on the broader JBI framework for systematic reviews, which emphasizes trustworthiness, relevance, and results [N1-F2]. In practice, the steps for using the JBI appraisal should therefore begin with careful item-by-item scoring, followed by reconciliation of differences between reviewers, synthesis across domains, and cautious interpretation when evidence is limited.

First, scoring each checklist item should be done systematically. The prevalence checklist includes questions such as whether the sample frame is appropriate, whether participants were sampled appropriately, whether the sample size is adequate, whether the setting and study subjects are described in detail, whether the data analysis covered the sample sufficiently, whether the condition was identified with valid methods, whether the condition was measured in a standard and reliable way, whether there was appropriate statistical analysis, and whether the response rate was adequate and managed appropriately [N1-F1]. These are the most relevant items for prevalence study design because they address sampling, representativeness, measurement, and analytic completeness [N1-F1]. Reviewers should answer each item independently and then compare responses, with disagreements ideally discussed before finalizing the appraisal [N3-F3].

When discrepancies arise, the JBI guidance recommends that reviewers discuss the items and agree on acceptable levels of information for a “positive,” “negative,” or “unclear” response [N3-F3]. This is important because prevalence studies can be particularly sensitive to disagreement on whether a study is sufficiently representative or whether the measurement methods are valid enough to support the reported estimate [N1-F1]. If two reviewers score an item differently, the discussion should focus on the study’s design and reporting, and the final judgment should reflect the reviewers’ shared understanding rather than a simple majority vote [N3-F3].

Summarizing bias risk across domains should be done by grouping the checklist items into thematic areas. For prevalence studies, the most relevant domains are selection/recruitment, measurement, and response bias, as well as adequacy of sample size and statistical analysis [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. The checklist explicitly asks about sample frame appropriateness and appropriate sampling, which is central to selection bias [N1-F1]. The response-rate question is central to response bias, while the condition-identification and measurement questions are central to measurement bias and outcome reporting quality [N1-F1]. The checklist also asks whether the sample size is adequate and whether analysis covered the sample, which is relevant to the completeness and robustness of the prevalence estimate [N1-F1]. For practical reporting, reviewers should tabulate the number of “Yes,” “No,” or “Unclear” responses across these domains and use them to characterize the overall methodological quality [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Overall confidence in findings is then inferred from the appraisal result, not from a single domain. The JBI systematic review checklist states that appraisal is used to inform synthesis and interpretation of results, and that reviews should be judged on whether the evidence supports policy or practice recommendations [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, this means that a strong appraisal—where the study is representative, well-measured, adequately sampled, and appropriately analyzed—increases confidence in the prevalence estimate [N1-F1]. Conversely, a weak appraisal—marked by missing or unclear items—decreases confidence because it suggests important design or reporting limitations [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The JBI guidance also notes that appraisal should be done by two reviewers independently and that discussions should clarify acceptable levels of information for each item [N3-F3]. This implies that confidence should be interpreted cautiously when discrepancies persist or when key items are unclear.

When using the appraisal in reporting and decision-making, the JBI framework recommends that the appraisal results be incorporated into the synthesis rather than treated as an isolated quality score [N3-F3]. For prevalence studies, this means that the reported prevalence should be contextualized by the study’s design limitations, the response rate, the measurement methods, and the adequacy of sampling and analysis [N1-F1]. If the appraisal indicates low confidence, the interpretation should state that the estimate may be unreliable or that the evidence base is too weak to support strong conclusions [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The JBI tools also emphasize that appraisal should support clinical decision-making in healthcare, so the appraisal should not merely describe the study but guide whether the prevalence estimate can be trusted for practice or policy [N1-F2].

Finally, when the study is too weak to score reliably, the JBI guidance suggests seeking further information or excluding the study from synthesis if the evidence is insufficient [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, this can occur when the sample frame is not appropriate, the sampling method is not described adequately, the response rate is too low, or the measurement methods are unclear [N1-F1]. In such cases, the reviewers should record the reason for exclusion and note that the study cannot be reliably appraised because key quality criteria are missing [N1-F1][N3-F3]. This is important because weak prevalence studies can overstate or understate the true prevalence, and their inclusion can distort systematic review results [N1-F1].

Overall, the practical steps are therefore: score each item independently, reconcile discrepancies through discussion, summarize bias risk by domain, translate the appraisal into confidence in findings, and use the appraisal in reporting and decision-making with caution when evidence is limited or conflicting [N1-F1][N3-F3].

This implies that confidence is not determined by a simple count of “Yes” responses alone, but by the reviewers’ shared judgment about whether the evidence is sufficient to support synthesis and interpretation [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, confidence is therefore tied to whether the study’s design, sampling, measurement, and analysis are sufficiently robust to support a reliable prevalence estimate [N1-F1]. If the appraisal indicates that the study is representative, well-measured, adequately sampled, and appropriately analyzed, confidence in the findings is higher [N1-F1]. If the appraisal indicates important limitations, confidence is lower [N1-F1].

The rating categories themselves are not explicitly labeled as “high confidence,” “moderate confidence,” or “low confidence” in the evidence provided. However, the JBI framework strongly suggests that these categories exist implicitly. The systematic review guidance says that appraisal should be used to inform synthesis and interpretation, and that recommendations for policy and practice should be supported by the reported data [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, this means that when the appraisal is strong, the findings can be interpreted with higher confidence; when the appraisal is weak, the findings should be interpreted with lower confidence. The prevalence checklist also asks reviewers to record whether a study should be included, excluded, or sought further information, which is an implicit confidence judgment [N3-F3]. Together, the evidence supports the idea that “Yes” responses generally indicate stronger support for confidence, “No” responses indicate major weaknesses, and “Unclear” responses indicate insufficient evidence to make a confident judgment [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## 3. How missing or unclear domains affect interpretation

Missing or unclear domains reduce the basis for confident synthesis. The JBI systematic review checklist emphasizes that reviewers should discuss acceptable levels of information for each item and that the appraisal should be used to inform synthesis and interpretation [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, if a key domain is missing or unclear, such as sample frame appropriateness or response-rate adequacy, the confidence in the findings should be reduced because important design or reporting limitations are not fully resolved [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that the checklist is used by two reviewers independently, which means that missing or unclear items can create uncertainty about whether the study is truly reliable [N3-F3]. Therefore, the interpretation should be cautious when a domain is missing or unclear, because the appraisal cannot fully support a confident conclusion [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## 4. How to interpret ratings when evidence is limited or conflicting

When evidence is limited or conflicting, the JBI guidance suggests seeking further information or excluding the study if the evidence is insufficient [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, this can happen when the sample size is too small, the response rate is too low, the measurement methods are unclear, or the sampling method is not described adequately [N1-F1]. In such cases, the reviewers should record the reason for exclusion and note that the study cannot be reliably appraised because key quality criteria are missing [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The broader JBI evidence also notes that critical appraisal tools are used to assess whether a study has addressed the possibility of bias in design, conduct, and analysis [N1-F2]. This means that, in the face of limited or conflicting evidence, the appraisal should be interpreted as indicating that the study is too weak to provide reliable evidence rather than that the study is definitively high or low quality [N1-F2][N3-F3].

## 5. Practical steps for incorporating JBI appraisal into prevalence study evaluation

Practically, the JBI approach to appraisal is structured around a checklist that asks reviewers to judge each item as “Yes,” “No,” “Unclear,” or “Not applicable,” with the purpose of assessing methodological quality and determining the extent to which a study has addressed the possibility of bias [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The first step is to score each checklist item independently, then reconcile discrepancies through discussion [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The JBI systematic review guidance says that reviewers should discuss each item and agree on acceptable levels of information for a positive, negative, or unclear response, ideally before independently conducting the appraisal [N3-F3]. This is important because prevalence studies can be particularly sensitive to disagreement on whether a study is sufficiently representative or whether the measurement methods are valid enough to support the reported estimate [N1-F1]. If two reviewers score an item differently, the discussion should focus on the study’s design and reporting, and the final judgment should reflect the reviewers’ shared understanding rather than a simple majority vote [N3-F3].

Next, the appraisal should be summarized by domain. For prevalence studies, the most relevant domains are selection/recruitment, measurement, and response bias, as well as adequacy of sample size and statistical analysis [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. Reviewers should tabulate the number of “Yes,” “No,” or “Unclear” responses across these domains and use them to characterize the overall methodological quality [N1-F1][N3-F3]. This domain-based summary helps identify whether the study is weak in sampling, measurement, or response management, and thus whether the prevalence estimate is likely to be reliable [N1-F1].

The appraisal should then be translated into confidence in findings. The JBI framework says that appraisal is used to inform synthesis and interpretation of results, and that reviews should be judged on whether they support policy or practice recommendations [N3-F3]. In prevalence studies, this means that a strong appraisal increases confidence in the estimate, while a weak appraisal decreases confidence [N1-F1]. When evidence is limited or conflicting, the study should be treated with caution or excluded if the quality is too weak to score reliably [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Finally, the appraisal should be used in reporting and decision-making with caution. The JBI tools emphasize that appraisal should support clinical decision-making in healthcare, so the appraisal should not merely describe the study but guide whether the prevalence estimate can be trusted for practice or policy [N1-F2]. When the appraisal indicates low confidence, the interpretation should state that the estimate may be unreliable or that the evidence base is too weak to support strong conclusions [N1-F1][N3-F3]. If the study is too weak to score reliably, the reviewers should seek further information or exclude the study and record the reason for exclusion [N3-F3].

## 6. Overall synthesis

In short, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for prevalence studies evaluates risk of bias by assessing whether the study is representative, adequately sampled, well-measured, and appropriately analyzed [N1-F1][N1-F2]. It identifies selection, recruitment, and response bias through the sample-frame, sampling-method, and response-rate items [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. It assesses measurement and outcome reporting quality through the condition-identification and measurement items [N1-F1]. It explicitly addresses prevalence-specific limitations by embedding those limitations into the checklist items most relevant to estimating prevalence accurately [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].

Risk of bias is quantified through the checklist item responses, interpreted through the reviewers’ shared judgment about whether the evidence supports synthesis and interpretation, and summarized by confidence in findings rather than by a single numerical score [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Missing or unclear domains reduce confidence, and when evidence is limited or conflicting, the study should be treated with caution or excluded if the quality is too weak to score reliably [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Overall, the JBI approach is practical, transparent, and evidence-based: it asks reviewers to score each item independently, reconcile discrepancies, summarize by domain, translate the appraisal into confidence, and use the appraisal in reporting and decision-making with caution when evidence is limited [N1-F1][N3-F3].
